title: Disclosing a prescribing error: IV paracetamol overdose in a low-weight patient

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information; patient safety
guidelineVersions: GMC/NMC Openness and honesty when things go wrong (June 2015; updated 13 Dec 2024)

related.id: MB-130 Duty of candour: disclosing a bile duct injury
related.why: The full candour conversation after a surgical complication with harm

A near miss: the professional duty of candour applies; statutory notification is unlikely

brief.scenario: Mrs Edna Threlfall, 84, is day 2 after a laparotomy for adhesional small bowel obstruction and is nil by mouth. She weighs 38 kg. When she was admitted, you prescribed IV paracetamol 1 g four times a day. She has had four doses in the last 24 hours. The ward pharmacist noticed this morning and the next dose has been held. Your registrar has seen her: she is well. On poisons service (TOXBASE) advice, bloods have been sent and an acetylcysteine infusion started.
brief.task: Speak to Mrs Threlfall about what has happened. The examiner may ask you questions at the end.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: You made the error. Tell her plainly, own it, apologise, and explain how her liver is being protected.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: "She feels fine, so there's no harm." Liver injury may not show for days.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Sit down, check she's comfortable, and ask what she has been told.

flow: Open and check what she knows

grid.label: Opening
grid.fail: Starts by standing at the bedside and reading out the incident, without checking what she knows.
grid.pass: Introduces self, sits, checks she is comfortable and whether she wants anyone with her, asks what she's been told.
grid.high: Checks the facts first (weight, doses, bloods, plan) and says early that he has something important to tell her.

grid.label: Telling her what happened
grid.fail: Vague ("a small mix-up"), minimises, or implies the pharmacist or nurses were to blame.
grid.pass: Plain words: the dose was too high for her weight and she has had four doses; says honestly that he prescribed it.
grid.high: Volunteers "I wrote the prescription" and gives the cause factually: her weight wasn't used for the dose. No excuses.

grid.label: Apology
grid.fail: No apology, or "I'm sorry you feel that way".
grid.pass: A clear, personal apology early in the conversation ("I am sorry").
grid.high: Apologises for the worry and extra treatment too, and doesn't let her play it down ("please don't worry about me").

grid.label: Harm, antidote and monitoring
grid.fail: Tells her there is no harm because she feels well, or cannot explain the drip.
grid.pass: Too much can harm the liver; blood tests of liver, clotting and paracetamol level; acetylcysteine protects the liver; tests repeated.
grid.high: Liver injury usually shows after about 2 days, so feeling well isn't reassurance; the drip can cause flushing or rash early: tell the nurse.

grid.label: The correct dose
grid.fail: Says 1 g four times a day is the standard adult dose for everyone.
grid.pass: IV paracetamol for adults 33–50 kg: 15 mg/kg a dose, maximum 60 mg/kg a day (not over 3 g). Pain relief continues at that dose.
grid.high: Works out her exposure: 4 g in 24 hours is about 105 mg/kg, and her correct dose is about 570 mg.

grid.label: Reporting and learning
grid.fail: Doesn't report it because she came to no harm, or leaves it to the pharmacist.
grid.pass: Reports it on the trust's incident system (feeds LFPSE) today and tells his consultant; explains the trust will look at how it happened to prevent a repeat.
grid.high: Names system fixes: weight on the drug chart, an e-prescribing alert for under 50 kg; offers her involvement in the review (PSIRF).

grid.label: Statutory duty of candour
grid.fail: Says statutory candour cannot apply because nothing has happened yet, or that it replaces telling her now.
grid.pass: Statutory duty applies to the trust for a notifiable safety incident (death, severe, moderate or prolonged psychological harm); his professional duty applies now.
grid.high: Harm not yet apparent can still count ("could result in"); moderate harm needs more treatment and significant harm; if met, notify in person then in writing.

grid.label: Her concerns, record and close
grid.fail: Leaves without checking understanding or recording the conversation.
grid.pass: Answers her concerns honestly, checks understanding, records the facts and apology in the notes, and gives a contact.
grid.high: Tells her she can raise concerns through PALS without affecting her care, and says he will reflect on it with his supervisor.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hi, I'm just here about a small mix-up with your paracetamol. Pharmacy flagged it, nothing to worry about.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mrs Threlfall: "What's this new drip then?"

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That's just a precaution. You feel fine, so there's no harm done.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mrs Threlfall: "Who wrote it up wrong?"

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's a busy ward. The nurses gave it, and pharmacy should have caught it earlier.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: She's well, so I don't think it needs an incident form. The pharmacist may have done one.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What is the correct dose for her?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: One gram four times a day is the normal adult dose.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Does the statutory duty of candour apply?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, nothing has actually happened to her, so there's nothing to disclose.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello Mrs Threlfall, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors. May I sit down? Are you comfortable? Would you like anyone with you? What have you been told?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mrs Threlfall: "Only that my painkiller's stopped and there's a new drip."

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I need to tell you about a mistake. Your paracetamol drip was prescribed at a dose too high for your weight, and you've had four doses. I prescribed it, and I am sorry.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Too much paracetamol can harm the liver. We've taken blood tests of your liver, clotting and paracetamol level. The new drip is an antidote that protects the liver, and we'll repeat the tests.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mrs Threlfall: "Will I still get something for the pain?"

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes, at a dose worked out for your weight.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I've reported this on the hospital's safety system and told my consultant, so we can find out how it happened and stop it happening again.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Can you tell me what you've understood? I'll write our discussion in your notes. The nurses can call me any time.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What is the correct dose, and does statutory candour apply?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: For adults 33 to 50 kg, 15 mg/kg a dose, up to 60 mg/kg a day. The trust has a statutory duty if this is a notifiable safety incident, such as moderate or severe harm; that depends on her results. My professional duty to tell her applies now.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello Mrs Threlfall, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors. May I sit down? Are you comfortable, and would you like anyone here? What have the nurses told you? I have something important to explain.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: When you came in, I wrote your paracetamol drip at the usual adult dose, but I didn't adjust it for your weight. So you've had more than is safe for someone your size. I am very sorry, for the mistake and for the worry and extra treatment.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mrs Threlfall: "Oh, please don't worry about me, dear."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's kind of you, but it matters, and you should know.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Too much paracetamol can harm the liver, and damage usually shows only after a couple of days, so feeling well doesn't rule it out. That's why we're checking your blood and giving an antidote, acetylcysteine. It can cause flushing or a rash early on, so tell the nurse if you notice that.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Your pain relief will continue at the right dose for your weight.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I've reported it and told my consultant. We'll look at why: for example, recording your weight on the drug chart, and a computer alert for patients under 50 kg. You can be involved in that review if you'd like.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mrs Threlfall: "I don't want anyone getting into trouble."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Reporting is about learning, not blame. If you want to raise concerns, PALS can help, and it won't affect your care. I'll record this in your notes, and I'll reflect on it with my supervisor.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Her dose, and is this a notifiable incident?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: She had 4 g, about 105 mg/kg; her dose is about 570 mg. Harm not yet apparent can still count. If she needs more treatment or a longer stay with significant harm, it's moderate harm: the trust tells her in person, then in writing.

failures.move: Telling her there's no harm because she feels well.
failures.consequence: Liver injury after paracetamol excess usually appears after about 2 days; false reassurance undermines trust when results change.

failures.move: Calling it a "mix-up" or blaming pharmacy and nursing staff.
failures.consequence: She is owed the true account of what happened and why; deflecting blame damages trust.

failures.move: Deciding statutory candour can't apply because nothing has happened yet.
failures.consequence: For NHS bodies, an incident that could result in moderate or severe harm can be notifiable; the harm must be assessed.

failures.move: Not reporting because she is well.
failures.consequence: Incidents with and without harm must be reported so the system gap (weight-based dosing) is fixed.

failures.move: Stating 1 g four times a day is correct for all adults.
failures.consequence: Repeats the error: under 50 kg the dose is weight-based.

recovery.when: She asks who made the mistake
recovery.line: I did. I prescribed it without adjusting for your weight, and I'm sorry.

recovery.when: You forgot to explain the drip
recovery.line: I should explain the new drip: it's an antidote that protects your liver while we wait for the results.

knowledge.fact: IV paracetamol, adults 33–50 kg: 15 mg/kg a dose, maximum 60 mg/kg a day, not over 3 g. Liver damage usually appears after 2 days, maximal at 4–6 days.
Acetylcysteine can cause anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, rash, bronchospasm), usually 15–60 minutes into the infusion.
Under 40 kg: reduce acetylcysteine infusion volumes (fluid overload, hyponatraemia, seizures).
Tell the patient as soon as possible, share what you know, apologise personally, and record it (paras 11–17).
NHS bodies: an incident that could result in, or appears to have resulted in, death, severe, moderate or prolonged psychological harm is notifiable.
"Could result in" covers harm that may appear later; it does not bring near misses into scope.
England reports patient safety events to LFPSE, usually through the trust's local system.

recall.think: A liver-toxic overdose: harm may not show for days.
recall.say: "I prescribed a dose too high for your weight. I am sorry."
do: Tell her now, own it, apologise
Report today; flag for candour review

numbers.meaning: IV paracetamol, adults 33–50 kg (not over 3 g)
liver damage usually becomes evident after this

recall.finish: Record, inform consultant, reflect; trust decides on statutory notification once harm is known.

sources.supports: Tell the patient as soon as possible (para 11); share what you know and apologise (para 12); what happened, what will be done about harm, prevention (para 14); apology is not admission of liability (para 15); personal apology, recorded (para 17); near misses: professional judgement (paras 21–22); report incidents, LFPSE in England (paras 23–25)

sources.version: Made 6 November 2014; current revised text, legislation.gov.uk (September 2026)

sources.name: Paracetamol 10 mg/ml solution for infusion (B. Braun): Summary of Product Characteristics (emc 15148)
sources.version: Date of revision of text 18 April 2025
sources.supports: Adults over 33 to 50 kg: 15 mg/kg per administration, maximum 60 mg/kg a day not exceeding 3 g (4.2); overdose: liver damage usually evident after 2 days, maximal at 4–6 days; N-acetylcysteine treatment (4.9)

sources.name: Parvolex (acetylcysteine) 200 mg/ml concentrate for solution for infusion: Summary of Product Characteristics (emc 1000)
sources.version: Date of revision of text 27 March 2017
sources.supports: Anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, rash, pruritus, bronchospasm), usually 15–60 minutes after the start of infusion; management by suspending the infusion; caution under 40 kg or fluid restriction because of fluid overload, hyponatraemia and seizures, so reduce infusion volumes (4.2, 4.4)

sources.supports: Concerned oral paracetamol in adult inpatients under 50 kg; the same learning applies to IV prescribing. Low bodyweight not recorded on the medication chart and paracetamol perceived as low risk; safety observation that electronic prescribing should alert when a patient under 50 kg is prescribed paracetamol

media.task: Read the prescription and the recorded weight before speaking to her
media.description: Inpatient drug chart excerpt: IV paracetamol 1 g four times a day with four doses signed as given, and a separate observation chart showing weight 38 kg

partner.opening: Mrs Threlfall is sitting up in bed with an infusion running. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Edna Threlfall, 84, a retired dressmaker who lives alone and is proud of managing. You are alert, a little sore, and slightly deaf in your left ear. Opening line: "The nurse stopped my painkiller this morning and put up a new drip. What's going on?" You are polite and tend to play things down. If told plainly and with an apology, you are calm: "Well, we all make mistakes, dear." If the candidate is vague, ask: "Who wrote it up wrong?" Hidden concerns, revealed only if asked how she feels or what worries her: (1) whether she will still get pain relief, as the wound is sore; (2) she doesn't want "anyone getting into trouble"; (3) she wants to know if her liver will be all right, because she hopes to be home for her great-granddaughter's christening in three weeks. If the candidate says there is no harm, later say: "But then why do I need this drip?"

reveals.trigger: Asks what she has been told
reveals.finding: "Only that my painkiller's stopped and there's a new drip."
"So it's to protect my liver. Will I know if something's wrong?"
"I want to be home for the christening. And I'm sore without the painkiller."
"I don't want anyone getting into trouble."

push.question: What is the correct dose of IV paracetamol for her?
push.expect: 15 mg/kg a dose, maximum 60 mg/kg a day and not over 3 g; about 570 mg a dose for 38 kg.

push.question: How will you report this?
push.expect: Trust incident system (feeds LFPSE) today; consultant informed; system learning such as weight on the chart.

push.question: Does the statutory duty of candour apply?
push.expect: Possibly: it may be a notifiable safety incident if it could result in moderate or severe harm; trust reviews harm; professional duty applies now.

curveballs.prompt: "Are you going to get into trouble, doctor?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Answers honestly that it has been reported so the hospital can learn, and he will reflect on it; brings the focus back to her care.
Tells her she is entitled to, explains PALS, and says it won't affect her care.

curveballs.prompt: The examiner says: her ALT is now rising.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Continues acetylcysteine as advised, escalates to the registrar and consultant, and tells her honestly; this may now meet moderate harm, so the trust's statutory process applies.
She was weighed, but the weight wasn't used for the dose; that's what the review will look at. Doesn't speculate beyond the facts.
